conversation.content: Let's design a real-time messaging system — think WhatsApp or Slack. It should support 1:1 chats and group conversations. What clarifying questions do you have?
How many users are we talking about? And is it just text messages?
50 million DAU, text only. Group chats up to 500 members. Messages should be delivered in real-time — as fast as possible. Let's start.

Okay. So the main thing is getting messages from one user to another quickly. I'd have the clients poll the server regularly to check for new messages. Every couple of seconds, the client sends a request asking if there are any new messages.

Polling every 2 seconds — with 50 million DAU, even if 10 million are online simultaneously, that's 5 million polling requests per second. Most will return empty. That's a lot of wasted bandwidth and server resources. Is there a better approach for real-time delivery?
Long polling? The client sends a request and the server holds it open until there's a new message, then responds. That way we're not constantly hitting the server with empty requests.

Long polling is better than short polling, but it still creates a new HTTP connection every time a message is delivered. For a chat app with rapid back-and-forth messages, that overhead adds up. What about persistent connections?
Oh right, WebSockets. The client opens a persistent connection to the server and both sides can send data at any time. So messages can be pushed instantly without the client needing to ask.
Good. So now you have 10 million concurrent WebSocket connections. Walk me through the architecture — how does a message get from User A to User B?

User A sends the message through their WebSocket to the server. The server stores the message in a database. Then the server looks up User B's connection and pushes the message through User B's WebSocket.

You said 'the server looks up User B's connection.' With 10 million connections spread across multiple servers — you can't fit all of them on one machine — how does the server know which server User B is connected to?

We'd need to keep track of which user is on which server. Maybe a database table or Redis hash — mapping user_id to server_id. When a user connects, we add the entry. When they disconnect, we remove it. So to route a message, we look up the target server in Redis and forward the message there.
Okay. But what happens when the WebSocket connection drops? Say the user's phone loses signal for 30 seconds and then comes back.
They'd reconnect. Open a new WebSocket to... the same server? Or maybe a different one since the load balancer might route them elsewhere.
Right, they could reconnect to any server. What about the messages that were sent to them during those 30 seconds when they were disconnected?

Oh, those messages would be lost because there was no WebSocket to push them to... unless we store them somewhere. I guess that's why we persist messages to the database. When the user reconnects, they need to fetch any messages they missed.
How does the client know which messages it missed? If it was last online at a certain time and reconnects, how does it know where to start syncing from?

The client could track the timestamp of the last message it received. On reconnect, it asks the server for all messages after that timestamp. But timestamps might have ordering issues... maybe we should use a sequence number instead? Like an incrementing counter per conversation, and the client tracks the last sequence number it saw.
Good. What about message ordering? In a group chat with 500 members all sending messages, how do you ensure everyone sees messages in the same order?

If we assign sequence numbers on the server side for each conversation, then every message has a unique position. All clients display messages in sequence number order. As long as the server assigns the sequence numbers correctly, ordering is consistent.
How do you generate those sequence numbers without them becoming a bottleneck? Multiple messages to the same group chat arriving at different servers simultaneously.

Redis INCR on a key per conversation? It's atomic and fast. For a 500-member group, the message rate per conversation is probably not that high — maybe a few messages per second at most. Redis INCR can handle thousands per second, so it shouldn't be a bottleneck.
What database would you use for storing messages?
Maybe MySQL? A messages table with message_id, conversation_id, sender_id, content, sequence_number, and timestamp. With an index on (conversation_id, sequence_number) for fetching messages in order.
50 million DAU, each sending maybe 40 messages a day. That's 2 billion messages per day. MySQL with a single table — how does that hold up over a year?

That's 730 billion messages a year. We'd definitely need to shard. We could shard by conversation_id so all messages in a conversation are on the same shard. We'd also want to archive or delete old messages at some point.
We're out of time. Any final thoughts?

I'd want to add push notifications for when the app is closed, and some kind of typing indicator feature. Also maybe message search using Elasticsearch. I realize I should have started with WebSockets from the beginning — the polling approach was a mistake.
Appreciate the self-awareness. You got to reasonable solutions on ordering and sync, but the initial polling choice and the reconnection handling were areas where you struggled. Thanks.

strengths: Recovered from polling to WebSocket and understood the reasoning
Good understanding of sequence numbers for message ordering
Honest self-assessment at the end — recognized the polling mistake
weaknesses: Started with polling instead of WebSocket — fundamental misunderstanding of real-time chat requirements
Couldn't articulate reconnection handling — messages would be lost without prompting
No capacity estimation until interviewer forced the database scaling discussion
Database choice of MySQL without considering write-optimized alternatives like Cassandra
No discussion of cross-server message routing strategy beyond basic Redis lookup
Zero discussion of group chat fan-out efficiency or read receipts
